Chapter 4: Deceit and Diplomacy—Broken Promises and the Making of New Borders
As the war dragged on, the gap between what was promised and what actually happened just kept getting wider. In London and Paris, diplomats were busy behind closed doors, drawing up secret deals—slicing the Middle East into British and French zones, all without setting foot in the desert. The Sykes-Picot Agreement, crafted far from the front lines, split the region right down the middle, completely ignoring the hopes and sacrifices of those fighting on the ground.
Out in the field, the scholar and his Arab allies pushed ahead—taking control of key towns, disrupting Ottoman supply lines, and winning battles that seemed to bring the promise of a brighter future. But with every victory came a nagging question: what would happen when the war was finally over? Would the Arabs get the independence they’d been promised, or were they just swapping one foreign ruler for another?
Back at British headquarters, things weren’t any clearer. Some officers talked about partnership and freedom, but others saw the Arabs as nothing more than a means to an end. The scholar found himself stuck in the middle—trying to bridge this growing divide. He wrote report after report, urging his leaders to keep their word, warning them that breaking these promises would leave scars that might never heal.
Meanwhile, other players were making moves in the shadows. French agents, determined to protect their own interests, were striking deals with local leaders. The Germans, even as they lost ground, tried to stir up resistance against the Allies. And American officials—watching from afar—wondered what part they might play when the fighting stopped.
For everyone living through this mess, the future felt shaky at best. Some people clung to the hope of self-rule, while others just braced themselves for disappointment. In the markets and mosques, rumors spread like wildfire—what did these foreigners really want? Once trust is broken, it’s tough to put back together.
As the end of fighting drew closer, the outline of a new Middle East started to appear—borders drawn with little thought for history or local ties. Old rivalries were frozen into brand-new states. And the scholar—worn out and disillusioned—could see that the freedom he’d dreamed of hadn’t arrived. Instead, the war had laid the groundwork for new conflicts, ones that would echo through generations.
